findings.claim: The final stanza turns the literal storm at sea into a picture of the speaker’s mind: “The night is dark, the waters deep, / Yet soft the billows roll; / Alas! at every breeze I weep — / The storm is in my soul.” The weather and her emotion become the same thing.
findings.problem: Contradicted by the source text quoted in the same sentence. There is no literal storm in the final stanza: the sea is explicitly calm — 'Yet soft the billows roll' — and the only storm is the internal one ('The storm is in my soul'). The stanza works by CONTRAST between the calm outer sea and the speaker's turmoil, not by the weather matching her feelings. Verified against the source text (Poem 1, stanza VI) and the Poetry Foundation text of 'A Song'.
findings.correction: The final stanza contrasts a calm sea with a turbulent mind: “The night is dark, the waters deep, / Yet soft the billows roll; / Alas! at every breeze I weep — / The storm is in my soul.” The billows roll “soft” and only a “breeze” blows, so the storm exists nowhere but inside the speaker — the metaphor gains its force precisely because the weather does not match her feelings.

findings.claim: The poem’s storm imagery becomes pathetic fallacy: by the final stanza, the literal storm at sea and the speaker’s inner turmoil are the same thing.
findings.problem: Same misreading of stanza VI. The source text states the sea is calm ('Yet soft the billows roll') and that only a 'breeze' blows; there is no literal storm for the inner turmoil to merge with. Presenting the ending as pathetic fallacy inverts the poem's actual contrast between a quiet sea and an agitated mind.
findings.correction: The poem's storm is internal, not meteorological: in the final stanza the billows roll “soft” and only a breeze blows, so the calm sea throws the speaker's declaration that “The storm is in my soul” into sharp relief.

findings.claim: This technique — describing nature so it reflects human feeling — is called pathetic fallacy. Williams builds towards it carefully: stanza V asks “Is pity in the faithless waves / To which I pour my woe?” — the sea is “faithless,” just as the lover risks becoming unfaithful to his priorities. By stanza VI, the outer world and the speaker’s inner world have merged completely.
findings.problem: The claim that outer and inner worlds 'have merged completely' by stanza VI is not supported by the source text: stanza VI sets a calm sea ('Yet soft the billows roll') against the speaker's inner storm. The sea is called 'faithless' in stanza V because it offers no pity, i.e. it refuses to reflect her grief — the opposite of pathetic fallacy.
findings.correction: Williams flirts with pathetic fallacy only to withhold it: in stanza V the waves are “faithless” because they offer no pity to the woe she pours into them, and in stanza VI the sea stays calm while the speaker weeps. The outer world refuses to mirror her feeling, so the storm is displaced entirely into her “soul.”

findings.claim: What literary technique does Williams use when the weather mirrors the speaker's feelings in the final stanza?
findings.problem: The question's premise is false against the source text: in the final stanza the weather does not mirror the speaker's feelings — the billows roll 'soft' and only a 'breeze' blows while the storm is 'in my soul'. Students taught this premise would misdescribe the stanza in an exam answer.
findings.correction: In the final stanza, what technique does Williams use when the speaker says 'The storm is in my soul' although the sea itself is calm? (Answer: metaphor)

findings.claim: {"q": "What technique does Williams use when 'the storm is in my soul' mirrors the literal storm?", "a": "Pathetic fallacy."}
findings.problem: There is no literal storm in the poem to mirror; the source text has 'Yet soft the billows roll' and 'every breeze'. The card teaches a factually incorrect reading of stanza VI.
findings.correction: {"q": "What technique does Williams use when the speaker says 'The storm is in my soul' although the sea stays calm?", "a": "Metaphor \u2014 the storm is internal, contrasted with the 'soft' billows."}

findings.claim: In the second part, you choose one other anthology poem from memory, without the text in front of you. Because Bright Star is printed in full in your anthology, it is also a strong choice for this task
findings.problem: Contradicts the stated assessment rules for J352/02: part b) asks students to explore in detail ONE OTHER poem from the anthology, i.e. a poem other than the named anthology poem printed above part a). If 'Bright Star' is the printed poem it cannot be used for part b), so advising it as a strong choice for that task would lead students to answer both parts on the same poem. (The lesson's own earlier sentence — 'if Bright Star does not appear on the paper' — shows the correct logic.)
findings.correction: In the second part, you choose one other anthology poem from memory, without the text in front of you. Note that this must be a different poem from the printed anthology poem, so if Bright Star is the poem printed on the paper you must write part b) on another poem from the cluster — and Bright Star is only available for part b) when a different anthology poem is printed.

findings.claim: Keats repeats “still” three times in close succession — “still stedfast, still unchangeable” and “Still, still to hear”
findings.problem: Miscount against the source text: 'still' appears four times in the sestet — twice in line 9 ('still stedfast, still unchangeable') and twice in line 13 ('Still, still to hear'). The two phrases the lesson itself quotes contain four instances, so a student repeating 'three times' in an exam answer would be inaccurate.
findings.correction: Keats repeats “still” four times in close succession — “still stedfast, still unchangeable” and “Still, still to hear”

findings.claim: {"q": "Which word does Keats repeat three times in the sestet to stress constancy?", "a": "'Still.'"}
findings.problem: Factually wrong count against the source text: 'still' occurs four times in the sestet (lines 9 and 13), not three.
findings.correction: {"q": "Which word does Keats repeat four times in the sestet to stress constancy?", "a": "'Still.'"}

findings.claim: The entire poem is a single unbroken sentence stretched across all fourteen lines. Dashes pile up instead of full stops, so the reader is swept forward exactly as the speaker is swept forward by feeling. The grammar itself refuses to pause
findings.problem: Contradicted by the source text of 'Now'. The poem is not one sentence: line 1 ends with an exclamation mark ('Out of your whole life give but a moment!'), line 10 ends with another ('This tick of our life-time's one moment you love me!'), and line 11 contains a question ('How long such suspension may linger?'). What is true is that the poem contains no full stops at all and runs on through dashes. Teaching 'one unbroken sentence' as a structural fact would be a demonstrably wrong AO2 claim.
findings.correction: The poem contains no full stops at all: instead of closing sentences, Browning piles up dashes, so the reader is swept forward exactly as the speaker is swept forward by feeling. Only the exclamations in lines 1 and 10 and the question in line 11 break the flow, and even they push the voice onwards rather than settling it.

findings.claim: What grammatical feature runs across all fourteen lines of 'Now'? — correct answer: 'A single unbroken sentence'
findings.problem: The keyed answer is factually wrong against the source text: 'Now' contains exclamation marks at the ends of lines 1 and 10 and a question mark in line 11, so it is not a single sentence. The verifiable feature is the complete absence of full stops and the continual dashes.
findings.correction: What punctuation feature runs across all fourteen lines of 'Now'? — options: 'No full stops at all, only dashes and exclamations' (correct); 'Four separate stanzas'; 'A strict ABAB rhyme scheme'; 'A repeated refrain'

findings.claim: {"q": "What structural feature makes 'Now' feel breathless and urgent?", "a": "It is written as one unbroken sentence across all fourteen lines."}
findings.problem: Factually wrong against the source text: the poem is broken by exclamation marks (lines 1 and 10) and a question mark (line 11), so it is not one sentence. It does, however, contain no full stops.
findings.correction: {"q": "What structural feature makes 'Now' feel breathless and urgent?", "a": "It runs across fourteen lines without a single full stop, driven forward by dashes."}

findings.claim: “Now” compresses a whole life into one instant, using a single unbroken sentence to mirror the speaker’s refusal to let the moment end.
findings.problem: Repeats the wrong structural claim. The source text shows exclamation marks ending lines 1 and 10 and a question mark in line 11; the poem is not a single sentence, though it uses no full stops.
findings.correction: “Now” compresses a whole life into one instant, using dashes and a total absence of full stops to mirror the speaker’s refusal to let the moment end.

findings.claim: Mastering: Perceptive exploration of the poem's single-sentence structure, paradoxical imagery of time, and physical climax, supported by precisely chosen short quotations.
findings.problem: Rewards a structural claim that the source text disproves — 'Now' is not a single sentence (exclamations end lines 1 and 10; line 11 asks a question). Students following this guidance would assert an inaccuracy in an AO2 answer.
findings.correction: Mastering: Perceptive exploration of the poem's unpunctuated, dash-driven flow (no full stops anywhere), paradoxical imagery of time, and physical climax, supported by precisely chosen short quotations.

findings.claim: Mastering: Perceptive analysis of the unbroken sentence, absence of a fixed rhyme scheme, and use of caesura and enjambment, linking these features precisely to the poem's ideas about time.
findings.problem: Two errors. (1) 'Now' is not one unbroken sentence (see lines 1, 10, 11 of the source text). (2) The poem is not without rhyme: every line rhymes, in an irregular pattern (moment/endowment, before/ignore, condense/sense, last/past, above me/love me, Sweet/meet, more/core). Published analysis agrees the scheme is irregular rather than absent.
findings.correction: Mastering: Perceptive analysis of the dash-driven flow and absence of full stops, the irregular but complete rhyme pattern that avoids Petrarchan or Shakespearean order, and the use of caesura and enjambment, linking these features precisely to the poem's ideas about time.

findings.claim: There is no octave-and-sestet turn, no regular rhyme scheme, and no settled metre.
findings.problem: Misleading on rhyme. In the source text every line of 'Now' rhymes: moment/endowment, before/ignore, condense/sense, last/past, above me/love me, Sweet/meet, more/core. The scheme is irregular and not Petrarchan or Shakespearean, but it is fully rhymed, not absent — as published commentary on the poem also states.
findings.correction: There is no octave-and-sestet turn and no settled metre, and although every line rhymes, the pattern is irregular (moment/endowment, before/ignore, condense/sense) rather than following any standard sonnet scheme.

findings.claim: After reading, explain how the missing rhyme scheme and constant dashes make the poem feel spoken rather than written.
findings.problem: The rhyme scheme is not missing: all fourteen lines of 'Now' rhyme in the source text, just in an unconventional order. Asking students to explain a 'missing' rhyme scheme trains a wrong AO2 observation.
findings.correction: After reading, explain how the irregular rhyme scheme and constant dashes make the poem feel spoken rather than written.

findings.claim: {"q": "Does 'Now' follow a regular sonnet rhyme scheme and metre?", "a": "No — it has no fixed rhyme scheme or set metre."}
findings.problem: 'No fixed rhyme scheme' is inaccurate: the source text shows every line rhymed (moment/endowment, before/ignore, condense/sense, last/past, above me/love me, Sweet/meet, more/core). The poem departs from sonnet order but is not unrhymed.
findings.correction: {"q": "Does 'Now' follow a regular sonnet rhyme scheme and metre?", "a": "No — it rhymes throughout, but in an irregular pattern, and has no settled metre."}

findings.claim: Short actions are listed one after another with no connecting words, building towards the moment the whole poem has been building towards.
findings.problem: The final line in the source text is 'While cheeks burn, arms open, eyes shut and lips meet!' — the list is asyndetic until the final 'and', which links the last two actions. 'No connecting words' is not quite accurate.
findings.correction: Short actions are listed one after another with the connectives stripped away until the final 'and lips meet', building towards the moment the whole poem has been building towards.

findings.claim: so that the speaker can “make perfect the present”
findings.problem: In the source text the line is 'So you make perfect the present' — it is the beloved, addressed as 'you', who is asked to make the present perfect, not the speaker.
findings.correction: so that the beloved will “make perfect the present”

findings.claim: the final stanza locks into a firmer rhyme between “brow” and “sheen” and “green”
findings.problem: Wrong rhyme pairing. In the source text the final stanza runs now / sheen / brow / green, an ABAB quatrain: 'now' rhymes with 'brow' and 'sheen' rhymes with 'green'. 'Brow' does not rhyme with 'sheen'. A student repeating this in an AO2 answer about form would be making a demonstrable error.
findings.correction: the final stanza locks into a firmer, fully alternating rhyme — “now” with “brow” and “sheen” with “green”

findings.claim: If Love and Friendship is the printed anthology poem, the first part of the question will ask you to compare it with an unprinted poem exploring a related idea
findings.problem: Contradicts the stated assessment rules: for part a) 'The paper prints two poems above the question: the named poem from the OCR Poetry Anthology and an unseen poem thematically linked to it.' The unseen comparison poem IS printed on the paper; only the part b) poem is unprinted. Telling students the comparison poem is unprinted would lead them to prepare for the wrong task.
findings.correction: If Love and Friendship is the named anthology poem, the first part of the question will ask you to compare it with an unseen poem printed alongside it on the paper, exploring a related idea

findings.claim: spring and summer arrive in the second stanza, winter in the third
findings.problem: Contradicts the source text. Winter is named in stanza two ('Yet wait till winter comes again / And who will call the wild-briar fair?'); stanza three refers to December ('when December blights thy brow') as part of its final imperative advice.
findings.correction: spring and summer arrive in the second stanza and give way to winter within it, while the third stanza turns to December and the advice that follows

findings.claim: examiners reward genuine comparison throughout an answer, not two separate mini-essays joined by “whereas”
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about examiner behaviour. The stated OCR assessment rules say only that part a) asks students to compare the two printed poems with three given bullet points; they say nothing about how examiners reward integrated versus separated comparison, and no per-question band guidance may be paraphrased.
findings.correction: The question asks you to compare the two poems, so plan to move between them on each point — ideas and attitudes, tone and atmosphere, and the effects of language and structure — rather than writing about them entirely separately.

findings.claim: A common mistake with short poems like this one is under-quoting because there seems little to say
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about candidate behaviour/exam frequency; nothing in the stated assessment rules or published OCR material supports it.
findings.correction: With a poem this short, make every quotation work hard: treat each word Brontë chooses (“scorn”, “deck”, “silly”) as a deliberate effect worth analysing.

findings.claim: “scorn the silly rose-wreath now / and deck thee with the holly’s sheen.”
findings.problem: Not verbatim: the source text reads 'Then scorn the silly rose-wreath now / And deck thee with the holly's sheen,' — the second line begins with a capitalised 'And' and the line ends with a comma, not a full stop.
findings.correction: “Then scorn the silly rose-wreath now / And deck thee with the holly’s sheen”

findings.claim: This friend is asked to look at their own hands — the title comes from this instruction, “looking at your hands.”
findings.problem: Wrong narrative/speaker detail. In the poem the title phrase belongs to the speaker's declaration of solidarity — 'And so / if you see me / looking at your hands / listening when you speak / marching in your ranks' — so it is the speaker who looks at the friend's hands. It is not an instruction to the friend to inspect their own hands. Verified against the poem text as reproduced in the Stabroek News feature on 'Looking at Your Hands' and the Caribbean Beat profile of Carter; the OCR teacher guide likewise gives the line as 'looking at your hands' spoken by the poet about the addressee.
findings.correction: It is the speaker who looks at the friend's hands: the title comes from his declaration that if the friend sees him “looking at your hands,” listening when the friend speaks and marching in the friend's ranks, it is because he dreams of changing the world.

findings.claim: The second stanza turns to look back at a shared past, before the third stanza shifts tense
findings.problem: Misleading account of stanza two. The second stanza does not recall a past shared by speaker and friend: it reports what the speaker has 'learnt / from books dear friend' about earlier men 'dreaming and living / and hungering in a room without a light' who 'dreamed to change the world' — a historical past of oppression and resistance encountered through reading. Verified against the poem text (Stabroek News; Roots and Rights reproduction) and the OCR teacher guide question 'What kind of past is the poet alluding to in the second stanza?'.
findings.correction: The second stanza turns to the past the speaker has learnt about from books — earlier men who lived and hungered “in a room without a light” and who dreamed of changing the world — before the third stanza shifts tense

findings.claim: Carter addresses a “dear friend” throughout the poem
findings.problem: Imprecise: the phrase 'dear friend' occurs once, in the second stanza ('I have learnt / from books dear friend'); what runs throughout is the second-person address to 'you'. As written, students may claim the phrase is repeated.
findings.correction: Carter names his addressee a “dear friend” in the second stanza and sustains the second-person address to that friend throughout the poem

findings.claim: Walcott writes Love After Love as a single unbroken stanza of fifteen lines, with no rhyme scheme and no regular metre.
findings.problem: The line count is right but the stanza claim is wrong. 'Love After Love' is printed in four stanzas of varying length (5, 4, 3 and 3 lines) — verified against published descriptions of the poem's form (SuperSummary: "15 lines arranged in four stanzas of varying lengths"; Shmoop's form-and-metre analysis notes four stanzas ranging from three to five lines, with line 9 enjambed across a stanza break). The single-block appearance in the supplied source document is a text-extraction artefact (the same flattening affects 'Morning Song', which is really six tercets). A student asserting 'one unbroken stanza' in an AO2 structure paragraph would make a false structural claim.
findings.correction: Walcott writes Love After Love as fifteen lines arranged in four short stanzas of uneven length (five, four, three and three lines), with no rhyme scheme and no regular metre. This free verse form suits a poem about breaking old patterns: it refuses the tight, repeating shapes that might suggest an unchanging relationship, and its heavy enjambment — one sentence even spilling across a stanza break — keeps the movement forward-looking before it tightens into short, sharp commands at the end.

findings.claim: The poem’s free verse, unbroken stanza and second-person address make recovery feel personal, direct and active rather than distant or theoretical.
findings.problem: Repeats the incorrect form claim: the poem is in four uneven stanzas, not one unbroken stanza (verified against published accounts of the poem's structure, e.g. SuperSummary and Shmoop, which both describe four stanzas totalling fifteen lines).
findings.correction: The poem’s free verse, short uneven stanzas with heavy enjambment, and second-person address make recovery feel personal, direct and active rather than distant or theoretical.

findings.claim: {"q": "What poetic form does 'Love After Love' use, in terms of rhyme and stanzas?", "a": "Free verse in one unbroken stanza."}
findings.problem: Factually wrong: the poem is free verse in four stanzas of uneven length (5, 4, 3, 3 lines), not one unbroken stanza — verified against published descriptions of the poem's structure. Learning this card would lead a student to make an incorrect AO2 structure point in the exam.
findings.correction: {"q": "What poetic form does 'Love After Love' use, in terms of rhyme and stanzas?", "a": "Free verse: fifteen unrhymed lines in four short stanzas of uneven length."}

findings.claim: Mastering: Sophisticated analysis of the poem's unbroken free-verse stanza, second-person address and shift from long sentences to short commands, linking form precisely to meaning.
findings.problem: The rubric rewards an inaccurate structural claim. 'Love After Love' is not a single unbroken stanza; it is fifteen lines in four uneven stanzas with enjambment running across the stanza breaks (verified against published form analyses of the poem).
findings.correction: Mastering: Sophisticated analysis of the poem's four uneven free-verse stanzas and enjambment across stanza breaks, its second-person address, and the shift from long sentences to short commands, linking form precisely to meaning.

findings.claim: The most direct denial of connection comes soon after: “I’m no more your mother” than the cloud that reflects sunlight without holding onto it.
findings.problem: Misdescribes the image in the source text. Plath's lines read 'I'm no more your mother / Than the cloud that distills a mirror to reflect its own slow / Effacement at the wind's hand' — the cloud condenses into a mirror (pool) that reflects its OWN gradual disappearance; there is no sunlight in the image. The gloss misstates what the poem says at a point students are likely to quote for AO2.
findings.correction: The most direct denial of connection comes soon after: “I’m no more your mother” than a cloud that “distills a mirror” in which it watches its own slow disappearance.

findings.claim: The cloud that reflects light without holding it
findings.problem: Same misreading of the source text: the cloud in Plath's simile reflects 'its own slow / Effacement at the wind's hand', i.e. its own erasure, not light. The matching item should describe the image accurately.
findings.correction: The cloud that reflects its own slow erasure by the wind

findings.claim: (parse failure)
findings.problem: Expecting ',' delimiter: line 1 column 2627 (char 2626)

findings.claim: she imagines a partner echoing a cartoon catchphrase — “Who Loves Ya, Poo?” and “Fozzy Bear, that’s who!”
findings.problem: Both allusions are verbatim in the source text, but neither comes from a cartoon: "Who loves ya, baby?" was the catchphrase of Telly Savalas's live-action TV detective Kojak (CBS, 1973-78), and Fozzie Bear is a puppet character from The Muppet Show. Minor imprecision in the cultural reference rather than a quotation error.
findings.correction: she imagines a partner echoing a 1970s television catchphrase — “Who Loves Ya, Poo?” and “Fozzy Bear, that’s who!”, mixing Kojak's catchphrase with a Muppet Show character

findings.claim: spend real time on both texts and both bullet points — ideas and attitudes, and tone and atmosphere — rather than writing about Fenton first and the unseen poem second as an afterthought
findings.problem: Contradicts the stated assessment rules for J352/02: part a) carries THREE bullet points, not two — ideas and attitudes in each poem; tone and atmosphere in each poem; and the effects of the language and structure used. Telling students there are 'both' (two) bullets risks them omitting the language and structure bullet, which is directly AO2-bearing.
findings.correction: spend real time on both texts and all three bullet points — ideas and attitudes in each poem, tone and atmosphere in each poem, and the effects of the language and structure used — rather than writing about Fenton first and the unseen poem second as an afterthought

findings.claim: For a poem chosen for the second, unseen part of the poetry question, the exact wording has to come from memory.
findings.problem: Mislabels part b). Per the assessment rules, the 'unseen' poem is the one printed alongside the anthology poem in part a); part b) asks for one other anthology poem of the student's own choice, which is simply not printed. Calling part b) 'the unseen part' risks confusing the two tasks. The underlying point (closed text, quotations from memory) is correct.
findings.correction: For the poem you choose in part b), which is not printed on the paper, the exact wording has to come from memory.

findings.claim: Raymond Antrobus’s ‘The Perseverance’ also finds meaning in an unglamorous, “sleazy”-feeling setting rather than a conventionally beautiful one
findings.problem: The word 'sleazy' is Fenton's, not Antrobus's, and 'The Perseverance' is a guide-only text from which only 'man overstanding', 'having the big picture', 'overstanding', 'perseverance' and 'serves' may be quoted. Placing 'sleazy' in quotation marks in a sentence about Antrobus could lead students to attribute it to his poem.
findings.correction: Raymond Antrobus’s ‘The Perseverance’ also finds meaning in an unglamorous setting — a local pub — rather than a conventionally beautiful one

findings.claim: She helped organise a millennial celebration at the Lincoln Memorial alongside composer John Williams and director Steven Spielberg, showing her standing across the arts.
findings.problem: Overstates her role. The OCR teacher guide says only that she 'contributed, with John Williams and Steven Spielberg to the White House millennial celebration at the Lincoln Memorial'; published biographies (University of Virginia bio; Yale News, 2007) record that for 'America's Millennium' (the White House 1999/2000 New Year celebration) she gave a live reading of one of her poems at the Lincoln Memorial, accompanied by John Williams's music, filmed for Steven Spielberg's documentary 'The Unfinished Journey'. She was a contributor and performer, not an organiser.
findings.correction: For the White House's 'America's Millennium' New Year celebration she read one of her poems live at the Lincoln Memorial, accompanied by music from composer John Williams, with the reading filmed for Steven Spielberg's documentary — showing her standing across the arts.

findings.claim: Every night the maid must wear her mistress’s pearls next to her own skin, warming them with her body heat before they are cool enough to place around her mistress’s throat for the evening.
findings.problem: Inverted and mistimed against the source text. The poem states the mistress 'bids me wear them, warm them, until evening' and 'All day I think of her' — the maid wears the pearls through the day, not every night — and she warms them so they are WARM when placed, at six, 'round her cool, white throat'. Saying she warms them 'before they are cool enough' reverses the poem's central heat-transfer image and would lose marks on the poem's controlling metaphor.
findings.correction: “Warming Her Pearls” is a dramatic monologue spoken by a lady’s maid in service to a wealthy mistress. All day the maid must wear her mistress’s pearls next to her own skin, warming them with her body heat until, at six, they are warm enough to be placed around her mistress’s “cool, white throat” for the evening.

findings.claim: Duffy writes “Warming Her Pearls” as a single unbroken stretch of verse, with no stanza breaks separating one thought from the next. The lack of division mirrors the maid’s relentless, circling obsession
findings.problem: Wrong form claim. In the source text the poem runs to twenty-four lines arranged in six four-line groups, and published texts of the poem (e.g. Poem Analysis, LitCharts) confirm it is set out in six stanzas of four lines each. There is no 'unbroken stretch of verse' with 'no stanza breaks'; the effect comes from enjambment running across regular quatrain boundaries, not from an absence of stanzas. A student asserting the poem has no stanzas in an AO2 answer would be factually wrong.
findings.correction: Duffy writes “Warming Her Pearls” in six regular quatrains across twenty-four lines. The tight, unvarying stanza shape mirrors the fixed order and routine of the household, while insistent enjambment carries sentences past the line endings and even across the stanza breaks themselves, so the maid’s relentless, circling obsession seems to spill beyond the boundaries that contain her.

findings.claim: The poem closes with an ellipsis, as the maid imagines her mistress “slipping naked into bed, the way / she always does...”
findings.problem: Contradicts the source text. The ellipsis after 'she always does...' is followed by 'And I lie here awake, / knowing the pearls are cooling even now / in the room where my mistress sleeps. All night / I feel their absence and I burn.' The poem therefore closes on 'and I burn', not on an ellipsis (there is also an earlier ellipsis at 'her every movement in my head...'). The lesson's own later paragraph and flashcard correctly give the last line, so the claim is internally inconsistent as well as wrong.
findings.correction: Duffy twice breaks off into ellipsis in the poem’s closing movement, as the maid imagines her mistress “slipping naked into bed, the way / she always does...” The trailing dots let her imagination run further than her words are willing to state outright, before the poem ends on the flat, burning admission “I feel their absence and I burn.”

findings.claim: The poem’s unbroken, enjambed structure mirrors the maid’s restless, circling obsession, and its dramatic monologue form lets her confess feelings she could never say aloud.
findings.problem: Repeats the incorrect form claim. The poem is twenty-four lines in six quatrains (source text line groupings; confirmed by published texts of the poem), not an 'unbroken' structure.
findings.correction: The poem’s six regular quatrains, constantly overrun by enjambment that spills across the stanza breaks, mirror the maid’s restless, circling obsession, and its dramatic monologue form lets her confess feelings she could never say aloud.

findings.claim: {"q": "Why does Duffy write the poem with no stanza breaks?", "a": "To mirror the maid's relentless, circling obsession."}
findings.problem: The premise of the question is false: 'Warming Her Pearls' is written in six four-line stanzas (twenty-four lines in the source text; confirmed by published editions). The card would teach students a wrong structural fact to reproduce in an AO2 answer.
findings.correction: {"q": "What is the effect of Duffy's enjambment across the poem's six quatrains?", "a": "The maid's thought spills past each regular stanza boundary, suggesting obsession she cannot contain."}

findings.claim: {"q": "What effect does the closing ellipsis have in the poem?", "a": "It lets the maid's imagination run further than her words state."}
findings.problem: The poem does not close with an ellipsis; per the source text the ellipsis at 'she always does...' is followed by three further lines ending 'I feel their absence and I burn.' The wording implies a false fact about the poem's ending.
findings.correction: {"q": "What effect does the ellipsis after 'she always does...' create?", "a": "It lets the maid's imagination run further than her words are willing to state."}

findings.claim: {"q": "What is the final line of 'Warming Her Pearls'?", "a": "'All night I feel their absence and I burn.'"}
findings.problem: Mis-states the line division in the source text: 'All night' ends the penultimate line ('in the room where my mistress sleeps. All night'), and the final line is 'I feel their absence and I burn.' Quoting the two as one line misrepresents Duffy's line ending.
findings.correction: {"q": "What is the final line of 'Warming Her Pearls'?", "a": "'I feel their absence and I burn.'"}

findings.claim: Mastering: Sophisticated exploration of the unequal relationship, analysing the extended pearl metaphor, the maid’s suppressed desire, and the effect of the unbroken verse form.
findings.problem: Directs students towards a false structural feature: the poem is in six quatrains, not 'unbroken verse' (source text line groupings; confirmed by published texts of the poem).
findings.correction: Mastering: Sophisticated exploration of the unequal relationship, analysing the extended pearl metaphor, the maid's suppressed desire, and the effect of the poem's six regular quatrains and pervasive enjambment.

findings.claim: Mastering: Sophisticated analysis of the poem’s unbroken verse and enjambment, linking form precisely to the maid’s obsessive, restless voice, with well-selected quotations.
findings.problem: Same false structural claim: 'Warming Her Pearls' is written in six four-line stanzas, so 'unbroken verse' is inaccurate and would mislead a student answering on form and structure.
findings.correction: Mastering: Sophisticated analysis of the poem's six-quatrain form and the enjambment that runs across its stanza breaks, linking form precisely to the maid's obsessive, restless voice, with well-selected quotations.

findings.claim: since no text is printed, examiners want to see short, exact quotations wrapped in analysis, not summary
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about examiner behaviour/preference. The stated OCR J352/02 assessment rules say only that part b) asks students to explore in detail one other anthology poem of their own choice in a closed-text exam, assessing AO1 and AO2; nothing published states what 'examiners want' in these terms.
findings.correction: since no text is printed, learn short, exact quotations and build your analysis around them rather than retelling the poem — AO1 rewards textual references used to support interpretation and AO2 rewards analysis of language, form and structure.

findings.claim: As the printed poem in the first part of the poetry question, “Dusting the Phone” would most likely appear beside an unseen poem about waiting, anxiety or longing for someone absent
findings.problem: Unevidenced prediction about the content of the exam paper. OCR states only that the unseen poem is 'thematically linked' to the named anthology poem; the theme of any future pairing is not published and should not be predicted.
findings.correction: If “Dusting the Phone” is the printed anthology poem, the unseen poem beside it will be thematically linked to it; focus your comparison on how each poet controls tone through structure and word choice.

findings.claim: is spoken by someone caught in the anxious early stage of a relationship, waiting for a telephone call from someone she loves
findings.problem: The source text does not indicate an early-stage relationship: the speaker refers to going 'over and over our times together' and imagines a future of 'A marriage. A full house. One night per week / in stranger's white sheets', suggesting an established but insecure, intermittent or long-distance relationship.
findings.correction: is spoken by someone in an established but insecure relationship, waiting anxiously for a telephone call from the person she loves

findings.claim: Antrobus also compares waiting to a parking meter, a <dfn class="term" data-def="A comparison between two different things using ‘like’ or ‘as’ to create an effect.">simile</dfn> that turns love into something measured, ticking down, and always running short of time.
findings.problem: The simile is misdescribed. In the poem (verified against the published text of 'The Perseverance', Penned in the Margins 2018, as reproduced by Poetry International and Literary Hub) the speaker is handed 50p to make him go away and pictures himself disappearing like a coin dropped into a parking meter before the time runs out. The vehicle is the boy's own vanishing and the minutes he loses outside the pub — not 'waiting', and not love being 'measured'. A student writing that Antrobus compares waiting (or love) to a parking meter would misidentify the comparison. OCR's own teacher guide refers only to 'the parking meter simile' and gives no such reading.
findings.correction: Antrobus also uses a parking-meter simile: handed 50p to make him disappear while his father drinks, the boy imagines himself vanishing like a coin dropped into a parking meter before the time runs out — a <dfn class="term" data-def="A comparison between two different things using ‘like’ or ‘as’ to create an effect.">simile</dfn> of the child's own erasure and of the minutes lost waiting outside.

findings.claim: {"q": "What object does Antrobus use as a simile for time passing?", "a": "A parking meter."}
findings.problem: Same misreading as the content: the simile is not a figure for time passing in general — the speaker compares himself, bought off with 50p, to a coin disappearing into a parking meter. The card as written would lead a student to misattribute the comparison in an exam answer.
findings.correction: {"q": "In the poem's simile, what does the speaker imagine himself disappearing like?", "a": "A coin dropped into a parking meter before the time runs out."}

findings.claim: Mastering: Analyses Antrobus's parking meter simile as a controlling image for time and patience, comparing its effect precisely with the central image in the unseen poem; sustains a balanced comparative argument.
findings.problem: Rewards a misreading of the simile. The parking-meter image works as an image of the child's own disappearance and of lost minutes (he is given 50p to vanish), not as a controlling image of 'time and patience'. Verified against the published poem text (Penned in the Margins, 2018).
findings.correction: Mastering: Analyses Antrobus's parking-meter simile as an image of the child's own disappearance and of the minutes lost waiting outside the pub, comparing its effect precisely with the central image in the unseen poem; sustains a balanced comparative argument.

findings.claim: The Perseverance also gave its name to Antrobus’s 2016 debut collection, which was shortlisted for major poetry prizes and named on several books-of-the-year lists.
findings.problem: Wrong publication year. Antrobus's debut collection The Perseverance was published in 2018 by Penned in the Margins (Poetry Foundation, poets.org, Griffin Poetry Prize listings); the '2016' date in OCR's teacher guide is an error and should not be reproduced.
findings.correction: The Perseverance also gave its name to Antrobus’s 2018 debut collection, which won and was shortlisted for major poetry prizes and was named on several books-of-the-year lists.

findings.claim: {"q": "In what year was Antrobus's poetry collection The Perseverance published?", "a": "2016."}
findings.problem: The collection was published in 2018 (Penned in the Margins), confirmed by the Poetry Foundation and poets.org; 2016 is two years out.
findings.correction: {"q": "In what year was Antrobus's poetry collection The Perseverance published?", "a": "2018."}

findings.claim: {"q": "What Rastafarian term does the poem's epigraph use for the father's wisdom?", "a": "Overstanding."}
findings.problem: The question presupposes that the epigraph's 'man overstanding' refers to the father. The epigraph is a quotation from Peter Tosh, and OCR's teacher guide explicitly leaves it open ('Is it the father or the poet himself?'), as does the lesson's own content_html. Framing it as 'the father's wisdom' teaches a closed reading the source does not support.
findings.correction: {"q": "Which Rastafarian term appears in the poem's epigraph?", "a": "Overstanding."}

findings.claim: Growing up hard of hearing and mixed race, and watching a father he loved struggle with alcohol, Antrobus asks what it means to keep loving someone difficult
findings.problem: Antrobus is deaf and writes about deafness; OCR's teacher guide states 'he writes about... deafness: his deafness was undiagnosed until he was six'. 'Hard of hearing' is not the term used of him and sits oddly beside the lesson's own later reference to 'his deafness'.
findings.correction: Growing up deaf and mixed race, and watching a father he loved struggle with alcohol, Antrobus asks what it means to keep loving someone difficult

findings.claim: The shift in tense and perspective around the third stanza also unsettles the reader’s sense of when events are happening
findings.problem: Imprecise as a structural claim. The poem mixes tenses from the opening stanza (present 'I wait' alongside the past recollection of what he had heard his father say); what changes at the third stanza is the move into remembered repetition. OCR's guide for this poem asks about 'the transition between stanza two and stanza three'; the 'change of tense in stanza three' question belongs to a different anthology poem ('Looking at Your Hands').
findings.correction: The transition between the second and third stanzas also unsettles the reader’s sense of when events are happening — the poem moves from a single evening outside the pub into remembered repetition, so that childhood and adult reflection overlap

findings.claim: To say the dark ‘winks the dark’ is smaller and playful, a brief flash rather than a flood.
findings.problem: The quoted span is on OCR's permitted list, but the lesson attributes it to the wrong subject. In Asghar's 'Lullaby' the phrase belongs to the image of the father's face — the mole on his lip's left side is what 'winks the dark' (text of the poem as published in 'If They Come For Us'; OCR's teacher guide simply asks students to compare 'light the underworld' and 'winks the dark' without assigning it to 'the dark'). Telling students the dark winks the dark is incoherent and would undermine an analytical point in the exam.
findings.correction: The phrase ‘winks the dark’ is smaller and playful: a detail of the father’s face flashes in the darkness rather than flooding it with light.

findings.claim: Keats wants to stay ‘stedfast’ forever watching over his sleeping love
findings.problem: This misreads 'Bright Star' against the source text. The speaker explicitly rejects the star's role of 'watching, with eternal lids apart' in 'lone splendour'; what he wants instead is to remain 'stedfast, still unchangeable, / Pillow'd upon my fair love's ripening breast', 'Awake for ever in a sweet unrest' and hearing 'her tender-taken breath'. 'Watching over' imports the very image the poem sets aside.
findings.correction: Keats wants to keep the star’s steadfastness but not its distance: he wishes to stay ‘stedfast’ while ‘Pillow’d upon my fair love’s ripening breast’, ‘Awake for ever in a sweet unrest’, listening to her breathing.

findings.claim: South Asian Muslim American poet and screenwriter, born in 1990, who co-created the HBO comedy series Brown Girls and lost both her parents before she was five years old.
findings.problem: Minor imprecision (repeated from OCR's teacher guide): 'Brown Girls' was an independently produced seven-episode web series that premiered on Open TV in February 2017 and was Emmy-nominated; HBO subsequently picked it up for development. It was not an HBO series as broadcast.
findings.correction: South Asian Muslim American poet and screenwriter, born in 1990, who co-created the Emmy-nominated web series Brown Girls (2017), later picked up by HBO, and lost both her parents before she was five years old.
